money_at_stake.basis: Resolved the occurrence: this is the SEC's proposed 'Regulation Crypto Assets' (Release No. 33-11434), voted out 2026-08-14, published in the Federal Register 2026-08-21 (matching the candidate's own date field, used as anchor_date since this AMBIENT candidate carries no occurrence block yet), 60-day comment period ending about 2026-10-20. Searched repeatedly for a dated, sourced dollar figure for the pool this rulemaking moves and found none that clears method section 1's bar. What the rule itself states is only per-issuer exemption ceilings (a startup exemption up to $5m over four years; a fundraising exemption up to $20m Tier 1 / $75m Tier 2 per 12 months), which are individual offering caps, not a market-size or capital-formation estimate, per the Sullivan & Cromwell client memo quoting the release text [2026-08-21]. Tried to reach the SEC's own economic-baseline analysis, which SEC proposing releases normally carry: sec.gov press-release and rules-regulations pages both returned HTTP 403 on fetch, and the Federal Register mirror redirected to a bot-check wall (unblock.federalregister.gov) that was not pursued, consistent with the CAPTCHA/bot-detection prohibition. Every third-party 'market size' figure found was rejected as non-citable: (1) 'digital asset custody market' reports from research-and-markets.com, Grand View Research, Mordor Intelligence and Business Research Insights quote, for the SAME year 2026, figures of USD 834bn, USD 953.5bn, USD 702.62bn and USD 1,047bn respectively, a 10x-scale disagreement with no shared methodology visible, the classic signature of templated market-research-aggregator content rather than measured data; (2) ICO/token-sale 'market size' sites (sqmagazine, coinlaw, icobench) were internally inconsistent within their own text (one page states both 'ICO market $5.78bn in 2025' and 'USD 25.2bn across three regions in 2025' as if the same fact); (3) a web-search synthesis reported 'up to USD 4.7 trillion in capital may now be unlocked... based on market capitalization of 16 identified assets... plus USD 2.9 trillion in institutional capital sidelined,' attributed to fintech.global, 2026-08-24; a direct WebFetch of that exact article found NO such figure anywhere in its text, only the same two exemption caps above, confirming the trillion-dollar number was fabricated in the search layer rather than published by the named source. No source clears the cited-or-NULL bar, so this leg is NULL rather than reaching for one of these numbers. The whole appraisal is UNRANKED on that account; the other three legs are still scored below because they inform which listed names to watch once (if) a citable figure appears, most plausibly in the SEC's own final economic analysis or in adoption data after the rule is finalized. Follow-up pass (2026-08-30, later session): went back to read the SEC's own proposing release directly, since a rulemaking of this scope normally carries a quantified economic analysis in the release itself, and the search-snippet layer above never actually opened it. sec.gov (both the PDF at sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11434.pdf and the 3-page official fact sheet) still returns HTTP 403 to a direct fetch, as before, and federalregister.gov still redirects to the unblock.federalregister.gov bot-check wall, not pursued for the same CAPTCHA reason as the first pass. A text-extraction proxy (r.jina.ai) reached the PDF around that block and confirmed the release genuinely carries an Economic Analysis part (Section IV, pages 183 to 277 per its own table of contents: A. Economic Baseline, ... C. Effects on Efficiency, Competition, and Capital Formation) and a Paperwork Reduction Act part with a subsection literally titled 'B. Estimate of Issuers,' exactly the place a quantified capital-formation estimate for this rule should live. But three separate attempts to have that one subsection's numbers quoted back verbatim produced three DIFFERENT sets of figures: first pass, '250 to 500' startup-exemption issuers per year, '50 to 100' fundraising-exemption issuers, '10 to 25' safe-harbor issuers; second pass, on the identical heading, 'approximately 400', 'approximately 100', 'approximately 50'; a web search then surfaced a third, more specific-sounding version, '130 offerings annually: 99 under the startup exemption and 31 under the fundraising exemption' plus '475 issuers... based on... 15 percent of approximately 3,165 crypto projects launched in 2024,' attributed in a dated, named-author legal blog (Brenda Hamilton, securitieslawyer101.com, 2026-08-19) to 'the Commission' and printed there as what reads like a direct quote. A verification pass then asked the same proxy-fetched release, verbatim, whether each of 3165, 475, 15 percent, 99, 31 and 130 offerings appears anywhere in its text: every one came back NOT FOUND. The SEC's own 3-page fact sheet, fetched cleanly through the same proxy (short enough to rule out the truncation that plausibly explains the inconsistent quotes above), contains no issuer-count or aggregate-capital figure at all, only the same three per-issuer offering caps already on record. Conclusion: the release most likely does contain the SEC's own quantified estimate of how many issuers and how much capital this rule is projected to move, since the section exists, is named, and sits exactly where a Paperwork Reduction Act burden calculation for this purpose always sits, but it could not be extracted intact by any tool reachable this session, and the specific numbers volunteered both by the direct extraction attempts and by a confident, named-author secondary source did not survive a direct presence check against the source text, the same failure class already on record above for the fabricated trillion-dollar figure. Citing any of these would repeat that defect with a more convincing-looking number instead of a less convincing one, so money_at_stake stays NULL. The concrete next step is unchanged from the first pass: re-test once the release becomes reliably readable in full, or once the SEC publishes the final rule's economic analysis.

public_reach.rationale: The rule's whole design routes the primary money the wrong way: an issuer uses the $5m or $75m exemption specifically to raise capital WITHOUT becoming an SEC-registered/reporting company, so the capital raised under it flows almost by construction to private, non-listed issuers rather than to companies a brokerage account can buy. The listed exposure that does exist is one step removed, in the custody and exchange layer that would service more issuances and more secondary trading: Coinbase (ticker COIN, not in this repo's market store) is the dominant listed pure-play, holding roughly 84% of US spot Bitcoin ETF custody assets (about USD 77bn of USD 91.7bn total) as of mid-2026. Beyond Coinbase, the custody build-out is coming from BNY Mellon, State Street, Deutsche Bank and Citigroup, all listed, but crypto custody is an immaterial sliver of each of those diversified balance sheets, which dilutes rather than strengthens the 'reach' claim for those specific tickers. Scored at 35, matching the method anchor for 'split with a large unlisted share': a real, if narrow, listed set exists one layer removed from the actual money, while the rule's direct beneficiaries (the issuers themselves) are structurally private.

In Tier 1 offerings, issuers may make offers and sales of up to $20 million of covered investment contracts in a 12-month period
In Tier 2 offerings, issuers may make offers and sales of up to $75 million of covered investment contracts in a 12-month period

capture_odds.rationale: Genuinely two-sided, so scored at the middle anchor rather than rounded toward either story. For capture: in January 2024, when BlackRock and Fidelity's newly approved spot Bitcoin ETFs triggered a fee war, Coinbase showed real pricing power by publicly stating it had no plans to cut its own transaction fees, choosing to monetize institutional custody and other services instead of competing on retail trading fees. That is demonstrated historical precedent rather than a current 2026 claim, so it is weighted as such; the more recent (mid-2026) reporting below confirms the same custody franchise is still dominant, which is the reason the largest banks are now targeting it. Against capture: that same mid-2026 reporting names BNY Mellon, State Street, Deutsche Bank and Citigroup as building competing custody infrastructure specifically because Coinbase's concentration and fee level are the target, which is the normal setup for margin compression over a multi-year horizon, not for a moat holding. Separately, the rule's actual first-order beneficiaries, the private issuers using the new exemptions, are not a capture case in the public-market sense at all: their capital raise becomes working capital for an unlisted company, not profit accruing to a public shareholder base. Evidence does not support a concentrated-oligopoly score, nor a pure commodity/price-taker score.

timing_fit.rationale: A formal process is genuinely moving, not merely proposed in principle: the SEC held an open meeting and voted to propose the rule on 2026-08-14, published it in the Federal Register on 2026-08-21 (this appraisal's anchor_date), and opened a comment window that a dated legal memo puts at 60 days, running to about 2026-10-20. But a dated report on that same process states the August 14 vote was procedural (whether to publish for comment, not a finished rule) and that final adoption is realistically expected only in 2027, and actual capital flows or measurable service-layer revenue for any reachable listed name would lag a final rule further still. That keeps this in the method's 'credible inside the window' band (60-anchor territory, scored slightly below it) rather than the 85+ 'spend committed and dated' anchor, since nothing is finalized, no capital has moved, and a change of SEC leadership or a legal challenge could still slip the timeline; it is comfortably not yet 'beyond the horizon' either, since 2027 adoption plus a realistic adoption lag still sits inside this repo's 2 to 5 year window measured from the 2026-08-21 anchor.

evidence.claim: The SEC's vote on whether to publish Regulation Crypto for public comment was procedural, not a vote on a finished rule; a comment period typically runs two to three months, followed by a rewrite before any final adoption, which the piece calls 'a 2027 story for compliance teams.'

source_excerpt: Not a finished rule. Friday's vote decides whether to publish the proposal and open it for public comment.
A proposal opens a comment period that typically runs two to three months, followed by a rewrite before any final adoption.
